concept.name: Early exercise
concept.definition: Early exercise is the exercise of an American-style option before its expiration date. It is rational only in specific circumstances — principally calls on a stock just before an ex-dividend date (to capture the dividend) and deep in-the-money puts (to capture the strike's interest value) — because exercising otherwise destroys the option's remaining time value.
concept.intuition: Exercising early is like tearing up an insurance policy to claim it today: you get the intrinsic value but throw away the remaining time value, so it pays only when something specific (a dividend, interest on the strike) exceeds that sacrifice.
concept.mechanics: An American call on a non-dividend stock should never be exercised early (Merton's result): selling the option always yields at least as much. Before an ex-dividend date, exercising an ITM call is optimal when the dividend exceeds the remaining time value; deep ITM puts can be optimal to exercise early because the strike cash earns interest immediately. Writers face early assignment randomly through the OCC's allocation process.
concept.formula: Rule of thumb: early-exercise an ITM call before ex-date only if dividend > time value of the call; never early-exercise a call on a non-dividend-paying stock.
concept.failure_modes: Retail holders routinely forfeit time value by exercising when selling would pay more; writers who ignore dividend calendars get assigned at the worst times and find their 'covered' position stripped of stock the day before ex-dividend.
concept.misconceptions: Early exercise is not generally 'taking profit early' — it usually leaves money on the table versus selling the option. The blanket rule 'never exercise early' is also wrong: dividends and deep ITM puts create legitimate exceptions.
concept.example: XYZ trades at $55 and goes ex-dividend tomorrow for $1.00; the $50 call trades at $5.10 ($5.00 intrinsic + $0.10 time value). Since the $1.00 dividend exceeds the $0.10 time value, exercising today to hold the stock over the ex-date is rational.
